blindSummary:
Trans visitors here face little risk. A new legal gender recognition act (July 2025) simplified the procedure and separated it from surgery requirements, but it still falls short of self-determination — a medical examination and a decision by the national health-and-welfare board are required. This was the last country in its region to reform its 1972-era legal gender recognition law.

One documented facility-access friction: a national swimming-pool chain's internal guidelines restrict trans customers' changing-room access — lawyers say this may violate discrimination law. The national crime-prevention council reports roughly 6,700 LGBTQI-related hate-crime reports, and the government is mapping digital threats against LGBTQI individuals. There are no documented severe incidents (no tourist-rape or mob-violence equivalent, and no Pride-targeted attack of the kind a neighbouring country has recorded). Bathrooms as such are unrestricted, and there is no criminalisation or rollback movement.
blindOutOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying foreign legislative-research library entry (April 2024) covers this country's parliament approving new acts on legal gender and medical procedures performed on genitalia.

Regional trans-rights organisation (July 2025): the country's new legal gender recognition act took effect 1 July 2025 - it simplifies the procedure (digital healthcare consultations, age limit lowered to 16, parental consent under 16) but falls short of self-determination: a medical examination and a decision by the national health-and-welfare board are still required, continuing to pathologise trans people; a religiously-affiliated party and the right-wing opposition vow to reverse it.

Public broadcaster (Oct 2025): a national swimming-pool chain stops trans people from choosing changing rooms - the company motivates its policy as being 'for all visitors to feel safe', a policy affecting trans swimmers' access to facilities.

National crime-prevention council report 2024:13: a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences with identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives, supplementing the country's hate-crime statistics.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2026 (covering 2025), chapter on this country: the capital's second LGBTI senior residence opened; the migration agency was instructed to improve consistency in LGBTI asylum claims and conversion-practices cases, though the main national LGBTI organisation reports continued reliance on stereotypical credibility assessments; asylum and migration legislation tightening, with concerns it may disproportionately affect LGBTI asylum seekers.

Academic journal study (2016) of LGBT policy in this country's armed forces, 1944-2014: archival analysis identifies two 'turns' (1971-79, when homosexuality was classified as a mental illness and framed as a security/blackmail risk, and 2000-09, shifting focus to organisational structures); no formal ban ever existed.
Foreign news magazine (2019): this country tied with two others at the top of a commercial gay-travel index of LGBT-friendly destinations - a top-tier ranking for LGBT travellers.
Expat news site (Jan 2017): this country to stop classifying transgender people as 'mentally ill' - the national health-and-welfare board announced the change, widely criticised as overdue.
blindLocalsOnly: The 2025 legal gender recognition act (medical examination still required) is a resident-facing process.
